chunks: Signals capacitors pass and block. The question: What sort of signals can capacitors pass through and block? What sort of filter behavior is this?
A capacitor passes signals that change and blocks signals that do not. Its impedance is infinite at DC and falls as frequency rises.
Moment by moment, i equals C dv over dt says current flows only while the voltage is changing. How it filters depends on where you place it. In series it makes a high-pass filter.
From the signal line to ground (in shunt) it makes a low-pass filter.
Think of a motion-sensor light. It reacts when something moves and ignores a room where nothing changes. A capacitor treats voltage the same way.
A steady level is the quiet room, so no current flows. A quick edge, spike or noise is movement, so a lot of current flows.
The picture is simple: real capacitors fade out gradually rather than switching on and off sharply.
Left: C in series, R to ground: the capacitor blocks low frequencies, so the output is high-pass.
Right: R in series, C to ground: the capacitor shunts high frequencies away, so the output is low-pass. Both corners are 1/(2πRC).
DC / AC: steady signals versus changing ones. High-pass / low-pass: a filter that passes high frequencies, or one that passes low frequencies.
Corner frequency: where the output is down 3 decibels, at f c equals 1 over (2 pi RC) . Roll-off: how fast the signal fades past the corner, 20 decibels per decade for one RC.
dB: a way to say how much a signal shrinks. minus 20 decibels means ten times smaller.
Use a 1 microfarads capacitor in series with a signal and a 10 kilohms resistor to ground. The corner is about 16 hertz. A 100 hertz signal comes through almost unchanged.
A 1 hertz signal comes through at about minus 24 decibels, roughly 6% of its size. A DC level does not come through at all. That is the whole idea.
"A capacitor blocks DC and low frequencies and passes high frequencies: impedance one over j omega C is infinite at DC and small at high frequency.
In series with a resistor to ground it's a high-pass filter; across the signal to ground it's a low-pass.
The corner is one over two pi R C, with a gentle 20 decibels per decade roll-off. In the time domain it passes changes, edges and spikes, and blocks constant levels."
